1.reason: Favor foundational separations, concrete circuit lower bounds and meta-complexity. Keep time, space and circuits visible rather than filling the prefix with NP variants.

2.reason: Favor basic primitives and reusable compression principles: sorting, terminal flow representation, sparsification and output-sensitive computation, before narrow graph-class classifications.

3.reason: Favor canonical barriers in synchronization, nondeterminism, expressive power and equivalence. Broad characterizations outrank model-specific closure questions.

4.reason: Favor compact decidability boundaries, algorithmic games, and foundations of proof assistants and program logic. Represent several foundations rather than only recurrence variants.

5.reason: Favor the limits of parallelism and locality, derandomization of matching, and lower bounds for powerful communication models. General primitives and streaming characterizations precede individual tradeoff improvements.

6.reason: Favor universal optimization and discrepancy barriers, exact feasibility, and dimension dependence. Fundamental geometric obstructions outrank refinements of one relaxation.

7.reason: Favor broad isoperimetric and embedding principles, algorithmic topology, and clean extremal geometric barriers. Representation costs follow general structural questions.

8.reason: Favor the relation between information and computation: compression, noise, expressive concept classes, statistical structure and cryptographic hardness. General learnability principles precede specialized models.

9.reason: Favor minimal assumptions for central cryptographic capabilities and information-theoretic limits. Keep secret sharing beside computational assumptions; place specialized efficiency improvements after broad primitive separations.

10.reason: Favor quantum computational power, local Hamiltonian complexity, entanglement and verification. Keep coding and capacity prominent without letting nearby QMA variants crowd out distinct phenomena.

11.reason: Favor structural laws of computation and explicit frontiers of mathematical knowledge. BB(6) supplies a concrete target alongside degree-theoretic structure; broad randomness and computable-analysis questions precede specialized definability fragments.

12.reason: Favor limits on general proof systems and the existence of a universally efficient proof formalism. Put central lower bounds and arithmetic strength before refinements of a single proof resource.

13.reason: Favor structural relations between algebra, information and communication. General compression, lifting and direct-sum principles precede exact costs of particular predicates.

14.reason: Favor the main fine-grained barriers and reductions that connect seemingly different primitives. Prefer a distinct algorithmic bottleneck to another variant of the same hypothesis.

15.reason: Favor removing randomness as a general computational resource and constructing objects at their natural information limits. Broad hardness-randomness principles precede a particular seed-length improvement.

16.reason: Favor whether parameterization truly enables tractability and whether iconic exact algorithms can break long-standing exponential barriers. Broad kernelization and width principles precede individual deletion variants.

17.reason: Favor principles that organize approximation hardness and prominent problems resisting even coarse guarantees. General thresholds and integrality phenomena precede narrow ratio improvements.

18.reason: Favor canonical online-information barriers and general selection principles. Keep scheduling and packing prominent in the remainder; narrower model-specific constants come later.

19.reason: Favor the worst-case/average-case bridge and statistical-computational gaps over the performance of one heuristic. Random combinatorial optimization is attractive when it exposes a genuine algorithmic threshold.

20.reason: Favor mixing at natural uniqueness or criticality boundaries and general principles of random exploration. Critical physical dynamics and combinatorial sampling take precedence over a specialized implementation improvement.

21.reason: Favor canonical approximate-counting barriers and the decision/counting distinction. General enumeration principles come before Gray-code variants and refinements of one counting algorithm.

22.reason: Favor global structural conjectures and the complexity of graph identity. Exact matching, flow and sparsity barriers lead the algorithmic remainder; close variants and specialized class restrictions follow.

23.reason: Favor universal adaptivity and strong data-structure lower bounds, followed by deterministic basic primitives. Long-standing structural conjectures precede improvements tied to one queue or hashing implementation.

24.reason: Favor robustness under arbitrary updates for core graph primitives and general limits of dynamic expressiveness. Broader dynamic metatheorems precede improvements for a particular data representation.

25.reason: Favor recovering strings from noise and fast comparison of sequences. General compression principles and metric structure precede specialized indexing tradeoffs.

26.reason: Favor whether fairness and truthful efficiency are achievable at all. Broad existence and black-box mechanism questions precede exact constants for specialized markets.

27.reason: Favor the cost of basic algebraic computation and general lower-bound/derandomization barriers. Keep broad algebraic decidability questions high, while placing restricted circuit refinements below the central separations.

28.reason: Favor computability of rational arithmetic and central number-theoretic algorithms. Broad lattice approximation and cryptographic foundations precede sharper constants in a particular reduction.

29.reason: Favor fundamental coding tradeoffs and multiuser information limits. Local decoding and computability of capacity remain central; already-known approximation targets rank lower as research questions while remaining eligible formalization tasks.

30.reason: Favor general characterizations of what can be learned from local access and the gap between testing and estimation. Strong structural properties follow before specialized query-model refinements.

31.reason: Favor general private learnability and the computational limits of releasing rich statistical information. Sequential privacy costs remain important but follow these broader boundaries.

32.reason: Favor general tractability classifications and the elementary promise of coloring an already three-colorable graph. Structural explanations and search/decision equivalences precede more restricted meta-problems.

33.reason: Favor the basic decidability and complexity of symbolic equations. General rewriting and unification principles follow; implementation-level refinements of restricted representations come later.

34.reason: Favor a syntax for efficient computation and structural characterizations of tractable model checking. General query semantics and enumeration principles precede specialized representation gaps.

35.reason: Both are compact, striking combinatorial conjectures. Prefer the sunflower question for its broader complexity connections, followed by the balanced-comparison principle for partial orders.
